theme: Make me to know your ways, O LORD
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 25. This is a prayer of David, an acrostic, in which he asks God to teach him his ways. Read it as a disciple’s prayer, the prayer of someone who wants to learn from the Master.
settingTheScene: Psalm 25 is a prayer of someone in trouble, surrounded by enemies and burdened by guilt, who turns to God for guidance and forgiveness. It is arranged as an acrostic, with each line starting with the next Hebrew letter. Coming after Jesus’ call to “learn from me,” it works as a prayer of discipleship: “Make me to know your ways, O LORD; teach me your paths.”
observation: “To you, O LORD, I lift up my soul” (v. 1).
“Make me to know your ways, O LORD; teach me your paths” (v. 4).
“Lead me in your truth and teach me, for you are the God of my salvation” (v. 5).
“Remember not the sins of my youth or my transgressions; according to your steadfast love remember me” (v. 7).
“Good and upright is the LORD; therefore he instructs sinners in the way” (v. 8).
“He leads the humble in what is right, and teaches the humble his way” (v. 9).
“The friendship of the LORD is for those who fear him, and he makes known to them his covenant” (v. 14).
“Turn to me and be gracious to me, for I am lonely and afflicted” (v. 16).
interpretation:
The psalm begins with trust: “To you, I lift up my soul.” The soul is lifted like a hand, in dependence. The psalmist asks not to be put to shame and says that those who wait on the LORD will not be.

Then comes the core request, repeated in several forms: show me your ways, teach me your paths, lead me in your truth. Notice the humility. David the king asks to be taught. He knows that guidance is not automatic, and that he needs God to show him the way. And the ground of his hope is not his own merit. He says, “You are the God of my salvation.”

He asks God to forget the sins of his youth and remember him according to steadfast love. This is the language of grace. David knows his past. He asks to be dealt with by God’s mercy, not by his record. “For your name’s sake, O LORD, pardon my guilt, for it is great.” He does not minimize his sin.

The central insight is verse 8: “Good and upright is the LORD; therefore he instructs sinners in the way.” God teaches sinners. The qualification for a student is not being good already but being humble. “He leads the humble in what is right.”

Verse 14 is a gem: “The friendship of the LORD is for those who fear him.” The word for friendship can be “intimacy” or “confidential counsel.” God shares his secrets with those who revere him. The psalm ends with a plea for rescue and for the redemption of Israel from all his troubles. It is a model for a new believer who wants to learn.
connection: Matthew 11:29: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart.” John 15:15: “I have called you friends.” Proverbs 3:5-6 says to trust in the LORD and he will make your paths straight. James 1:5 promises wisdom to those who ask. Psalm 119:105 says his word is a lamp to our feet. Isaiah 30:21 promises a voice saying, “This is the way, walk in it.” Romans 8:1: there is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
application:
Make verses 4 and 5 your daily morning prayer for a week.

Bring a specific decision to God and ask him to show you the way. Listen through his word.

Confess one sin from your past that still weighs on you, and trust his steadfast love to remember you.
prayerPrompts: Lift up your soul to God, and tell him what you want to know of his ways.
Ask him to lead you in his truth.
Ask him not to remember the sins of your youth.
